source.title: Rank-1 LoRAs Encode Interpretable Reasoning Signals
source.authors: Jake Ward; P. Riechers; Adam Shai

page_placements.theme: Many units in other domains and architectures lack a single-concept description

record.tranche_reason: Measures and classifies polysemanticity in sampled transformer MLP neurons using an LLM-based interpretation pipeline, rather than the original sources’ method.
record.gate_note: The study reports a comparison of interpretability classifications for sampled base-model MLP neurons and LoRA activations, which bears on V2. Benchmark scores, ablation effects, and SAE feature results do not measure the claim versions’ neuron polysemanticity. The authors note that their automated interpretation and categorization methods may fail to identify features’ true roles.
record.test_reason: An LLM autointerpretation pipeline classifies sampled MLP neurons of Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct as monosemantic, fuzzy or polysemantic. That gives a rate of polysemantic MLP neurons in a transformer LM, which bears on V2. The neurons are only a baseline for the LoRA analysis and the method differs from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude LoRA directions are interpretable and roughly as often monosemantic as sampled MLP neurons. They caution that LLM autointerpretation may miss features' true roles. They draw no conclusion about MLP-neuron polysemanticity itself.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LLM-generated interpretations and classifications of top-activating examples for sampled neurons and adapter directions; does not reproduce the original sources’ analysis method.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors say the SAE categorization methodology is subjective and sensitive to prompt verbiage; they do not report a comparison across prompts or scoring methods for the neuron polysemanticity measure.

fits_no_version.finding: Rank-1 LoRA adapter directions get monosemantic/fuzzy/polysemantic classifications similar to sampled MLP neurons (49.1/28.5/22.4% vs 46.9/32.9/20.2%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rank-1 LoRA adapter directions are about as often monosemantic as MLP neurons under LLM autointerpretation.

record.problems: Only one model is studied, and only the first 60 neurons of each MLP are sampled. Classifications rely on LLM-generated explanations of top-activating examples, which the authors say may fail to uncover features’ true roles. The classification percentages are shown in Figure 1 rather than stated in the prose.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were reported. Benchmark performance, component ablations, and SAE feature analyses were not included because they do not measure the neuron polysemanticity named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Variation across layers (no per-layer breakdown is reported), other language models, and neurons beyond the first 60 per MLP.
Classification depends on top-64 activating contexts and one LLM judge prompt. Neither the activation range nor the scoring method is varied, so measurement dependence is not tested.
No causal account of polysemanticity is tested.
No causal account of polysemanticity is tested.
No comparison across architectures or activation functions.
Polysemantic neurons are not re-examined with other tools.

record.verdict_notes: The prose says SAE features are 62% cleanly monosemantic, 'up from 22% of LoRA features'. That conflicts with Figure 1's 49.1% monosemantic for LoRA; 22.4% is the LoRA polysemantic share. Treat the prose figure with caution. MLP neuron counts are not stated; the sample is 60 per MLP across 64 layers. No uncertainty is reported and only one model is studied.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and mixed visual inputs.
Layer-by-layer variation, other language models, and direct independent verification that the classified examples are unrelated contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse features being packed together under capacity pressure.
Whether polysemanticity arises from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Changes in polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures, or regularization, and performance costs of reducing it.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect shared features or related offshoots rather than unrelated mixtures.
Whether changing the activation range or explanation-scoring method changes polysemanticity classifications.

rows.subject: Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Classified sampled base-model MLP neurons from their max-activating examples using an LLM interpretation pipeline.
rows.note: Figure 1 labels the base MLP categories as 46.9% monosemantic, 32.9% fuzzy, and 20.2% polysemantic. The prose says LoRA activations have roughly the same likelihood as MLP neurons to be monosemantic, but does not describe the base-model polysemantic share in words.
rows.check: The value can be read from Figure 1's labels: 20.2% polysemantic, 32.9% fuzzy, 46.9% monosemantic. It should be recorded as 20.2% polysemantic (class 2), not 'figure only'. State should be partial, not cannot_determine: about one in five sampled neurons is judged polysemantic, a minority rather than a large share. The fuzzy category ('broad or noisy' but all examples fit) is not polysemantic by the study's own rubric. Sample: first 60 neurons per MLP; judge: gpt-5-mini on top-64 contexts.

source_check.correct: Figure 1 (left) bar labels, read from the page 3 render: MLP neurons are 20.2% Monosemantic (0), 32.9% Fuzzy (1) and 46.9% Polysemantic (2). Value = 46.9% polysemantic, readable from the bar labels. For V2's share part the state should be observed: nearly half are judged polysemantic and only 20.2% cleanly monosemantic. The layer part is untested because results are pooled with no per-layer breakdown.
